facts.text: Producer Roger Corman reportedly insisted star Lana Clarkson be cast because she drew more fan mail than any other starlet in his stable.
Roger Corman already filmed Poe's "Morella" as the first segment of his 1962 anthology Tales of Terror. This 1990 version is a much racier remake.
Star Nicole Eggert was only 17 during production and needed a legal guardian on set, even though she plays both a mother and her grown daughter.
Mondo Digital calls the film a T&A-packed riff on Mario Bava's 1960 Black Sunday, which is directly quoted in the opening and used as a story template.
Roger Corman's company kept the budget under $1 million by reusing sets built for other Concorde Pictures productions.
Director Jim Wynorski cast David McCallum as a fan of The Man from U.N.C.L.E. He had also cast McCallum's U.N.C.L.E. co-star Robert Vaughn in Wynorski's Transylvania Twist.
At the height of The Man from U.N.C.L.E., David McCallum got more fan mail than any actor in MGM history, including Clark Gable and Elvis Presley.
Wynorski has said he wanted a blend of French-film atmosphere and Hammer horror, using gradation lenses for mood and soft lenses for a smoky look.
The film began shooting September 13, 1989 in Los Angeles under the misspelled title The Haunting of Maurella.
Deborah Dutch turned down nude work until she posed for Playboy. Soon after, the actress cast as the Serving Girl no-showed, and Wynorski offered Dutch the part if she'd do a nude bath scene.
Deborah Dutch lay motionless on a cold concrete floor for over an hour covered in fake blood for her bathtub death, then crew rinsed her off with buckets of warm water.
Lana Clarkson did many of her own stunts in this film, including the scenes with heavy pyrotechnics.
The character Miles Archer, played by Brewster Gold, was invented for the film. His name nods to the murdered partner in The Maltese Falcon.
Gideon Locke, David McCallum's character, is reportedly named after philosopher John Locke, whose ideas influenced Edgar Allan Poe.
The role of Morella and daughter Lenora was reportedly first offered to Traci Lords before Nicole Eggert got it.
Variety's reviewer "Advo." wrote: "Nudity, lesbianism, softcore sex, beer barrel-breasted babes: The Haunting of Morella has it all." But not enough for the box office.
Director Jim Wynorski made this and Transylvania Twist back to back for Roger Corman.
Daily Variety said the film opened "timidly" in only sixty Midwest theaters in February 1990, with ticket sales "weak," "tepid" and "dismal."
The film grossed just $599,951 at the U.S. box office. Its Los Angeles premiere didn't come until June 22, 1990, four months after Detroit.
Richard Scheib of Moria gave it one star, saying it treats Poe's story as "the barest of bones" and adds a confusing second plot about the governess's sacrifices.
Mondo Digital notes Steve Mitchell, a writer on Wynorski's Chopping Mall, worked on this film and served as second unit director.
Wynorski isn't credited onscreen as a writer, but Variety and other sources said he wrote it. He reportedly co-wrote with longtime partner R.J. Robertson.
Lana Clarkson got her SAG card at 18 in Fast Times at Ridgemont High, where she was picked from a line of extras to play teacher Mr. Vargas' beautiful blonde wife.
The Motion Picture Guide called it "nothing more than an excuse for its female characters to take off their clothes and kill each other."
Maria Ford, who plays Diane, was a former Las Vegas showgirl. She was reportedly considered for roles in Showgirls and Under Siege and was first choice for a part in Jason Goes to Hell.
The Morella corpse prop was designed and built by Dean and Star Jones.
Nicole Eggert went on to play Summer Quinn on Baywatch. Earlier she was Jamie Powell on the sitcom Charles in Charge.
David McCallum later played medical examiner Dr. Donald "Ducky" Mallard on NCIS for 20 seasons, until his death in 2023.
According to Wikipedia, Wynorski's softcore horror film The Witches of Breastwick was the subject of the 2009 documentary Popatopolis, named for his pseudonym Tom Popatopolous.
Corman later reused a crimson-soaked hellscape sequence from this film and recreated it nearly beat for beat in his 1995 movie Haunted Symphony, shot in Moscow.
The film reportedly went unreleased in the U.K., one reason it never got the cult reputation of other Corman titles there.
Lana Clarkson appeared in Scarface (1983). In 2013 Al Pacino played Phil Spector, the man convicted of killing her in 2003, in the HBO film Phil Spector.
Christopher Halsted, who plays Guy Chapman, later appeared in Star Trek: The Next Generation and Star Trek: Deep Space Nine.
The film's tagline was "Crucified, blinded and buried... Now she's back!"
